paras: The attack on Joe Williams and Earnest Griffin took place on the night of August 12, 1903, near the Virginia City mines in southern Jefferson County, Alabama, when Williams, a Black man, was shot and seriously wounded and Griffin, also Black, was beaten into insensibility. The assault came during a United Mine Workers strike at the mines, and a dispatch to the New York Tribune described the attackers as a mob that included a white woman. Three white men were charged with assault with intent to murder and highway robbery, but within two weeks the cases were dropped and one defendant was acquitted.

Virginia City was a mining camp near Birmingham where union miners were on strike while other men continued to work. A few days before the attack, according to a Birmingham dispatch to the Tribune, men were alleged to have surrounded the Black quarters at the mines on two successive nights and fired a volley into the houses each night, wounding one man. In the same dispatch, a Black man who had been on guard duty said miners had taken him into the woods and threatened to lynch him, then shot and wounded him as he returned to camp. The sheriff sent twenty-five deputies after that trouble.

On the night of August 12, Joe Williams was shot about a mile from Virginia City, and Earnest Griffin was beaten. The Montgomery Advertiser's Birmingham report placed the shooting on the road from Virginia City to Bessemer. On August 14 the Advertiser said the attackers were not known, while the Tribune's dispatch spoke of a 'crowd of assailants' and said a white woman was 'said to have been' among them. Four deputy sheriffs went to the mines the next day, and the Tribune reported that 'many additional deputies' arrived that evening, that the miners were 'heavily armed', and that serious trouble was feared.

By August 14, two white men had been arrested in connection with the shooting, charged with assault with intent to murder and highway robbery, and deputies were to stay at the mines for several days. The Advertiser of August 18 named the defendants as Rufe and Lil Morrison and Frank Jones, white men arrested at the Virginia City mines, who had made bond of $500 on the robbery charges and $200 on the assault charge. Their preliminary hearing was set before Justice Tillman at Bessemer, and the report tied the charges to the strike without naming Williams or Griffin.

On August 22 the Advertiser reported that the cases, which it said had been 'preferred by negroes', were nol prossed in Justice Tillman's court. Three days later it reported that Lil Morrison had been acquitted of the same charges before Justice Benners, with the strike still on and about half the miners still working. In October, a Frank Jones and a Lil Morrison were among union miners summoned before the chancery court for allegedly violating an injunction that barred named union members from the Alabama Steel and Wire Company's property at Virginia City. The coverage does not report whether Williams recovered or any further prosecution.

The attack received brief notice in the white press, and no Black-press report of it was found. The New York Tribune ran its Birmingham wire under the headline 'Renew Attacks on Negroes' with the deck 'White Woman in Mob That Shoots Black Miners', following its August 11 story 'Miners Shoot at Negroes'. The Montgomery Advertiser carried the story as strike news under 'Trouble at Mines' and 'Virginia City Troubles', and it was the only paper found to name the victims.

Its later items followed the defendants rather than the victims. Under the headline 'Accused of Robbery', the August 18 report described the Morrison brothers as 'well known men in this County' and said they were 'not bad men by any means'. Elsewhere the episode surfaced only in digest form, as when a Kentucky weekly reported on August 20 that 'serious trouble broke out' at the Virginia City mines during the strike.

Reports differ on who carried out the attack: the Tribune's dispatch described a crowd that included a white woman, while the Advertiser first said the attackers were unknown. The Advertiser later reported two white men arrested and then named three defendants. The robbery charge cast the case partly as a holdup on the road, while the Tribune and the Advertiser's first report placed it within the strike. The Advertiser also reported both that the cases were nol prossed in Justice Tillman's court and that Lil Morrison was acquitted before Justice Benners, without explaining the two outcomes.

conflicts.note: The later Advertiser reports (A5, A7, A8) tie the charges to the strike but do not name Williams or Griffin; A4 links the two arrests to the Aug. 12 shooting, so the identity of the three named men with the attackers is likely but rests on that link.
